\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more information.

Prior work found trace utility to be task-dependent \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks where output noise confounds the analysis.
Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, and controlled component ablation directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning.
This approach aligns with recent *ACL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.

We present a systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we evaluate four models across three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

The central result: complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone, while compact exception events achieve near-perfect accuracy (${\geq}$99\%) across all four models---an 18--23pp gap (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
A simple regex exploiting a format marker matches this ceiling, so the interesting question is not why exceptions help but \emph{why complete traces hurt}.
Marker removal collapses the regex to near-chance while SFT retains $>$97\%; cross-dataset transfer confirms SFT acquires diagnostic patterns beyond format matching (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

Gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution; content quality at inference accounts for the majority (\S\ref{sec:density}).
Training dynamics corroborate this: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates without convergence (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp performance transition near 512 tokens, coinciding with the first appearance of structured execution markers (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

While exception events structurally encode verdict direction (exception present typically implies failure), the non-trivial finding is that providing strictly more information (complete traces containing all exception data) degrades performance by 18--23pp.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy despite containing all diagnostic information}: across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone (${\sim}$73--76\%) while exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.33\%, an 18--23pp gap (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}). Training dynamics show the mechanism: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates without stable convergence (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).

\item \textbf{Systematic quantification of semantic vs.\ format-marker contribution}: marker removal collapses a format-exploiting regex from 99.33\% to 28.49\% (69pp) while SFT drops only 2pp (99.83\%$\to$97.65\%); bidirectional cross-dataset transfer (99.4--100\%) shows the learned signal generalizes (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

\item \textbf{An empirical two-tier signal hierarchy with a practical trace selection strategy}: Tier~1 (exceptions, assertions; ${\geq}$98.53\%) dominates Tier~2 (loop compression; 77--86\%) by 12+pp with non-overlapping CIs; the Tier~2 lift is significant for 3 of 4 models (CodeLlama \texttt{loop\_only}: +0.93pp, n.s.). A sharp performance transition at ${\sim}$512 tail tokens yields a practical fallback (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

\item \textbf{Mechanistic decomposition of the full-trace degradation}: gradient masking on \texttt{exception\_only} (mean $-$0.61pp under 99.8\% mask, 3 seeds) attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the 18pp gap to gradient dilution; content quality at inference accounts for the majority, though forward-pass attention is an unquantified residual. A complementary label-only ablation on the Qwen family yields a directionally consistent but confounded upper bound (${\leq}$26\%) (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\end{enumerate}

We evaluate across two research questions:
(1)~Why do complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy despite containing all diagnostic information?
(2)~Which trace components carry the verdict signal, and how does their density affect learning?
All experiments use $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% CIs.\footnote{Problem-level partition (472 train / 119 test, zero crossover; \S\ref{sec:dataset}). \texttt{exception\_only} duplicates (48.99\% test; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}) arise from within-problem variants; deduplication yields negligible ($<$0.1pp) delta.}

Individual exception subcomponents (type, stacktrace, message) each independently achieve ${\geq}$99.50\%, indicating that the binary presence of an exception event, rather than any specific subcomponent, drives Tier~1 performance (Appendix~\ref{sec:exc_subcomponent}).
The Tier~1/2 boundary is unambiguous: the lowest Tier~1 condition (\texttt{ae\_only} on DeepSeek, 98.53\%$\pm$0.30, 2 seeds) exceeds the highest Tier~2 (\texttt{loop\_only} on Qwen-7B, 86.05\%, CI [83.97, 87.96]) by 12.48\,pp with non-overlapping CIs (gap statistic supports $k{=}2$ clusters, silhouette ${\geq}$0.74).
Tier~2 \texttt{loop\_only} lifts over \texttt{no\_trace} are model-dependent: Qwen +10.92pp (7B) and +7.19pp (1.5B); DeepSeek +6.95pp; CodeLlama +0.93pp (n.s.).
\paragraph{Rule-based baseline comparison.}
The strongest non-trivial regex heuristic (B4: exception class name matching; Table~\ref{tab:regex}) achieves 93.61\% accuracy (F1=0.876), trailing SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%, F1=0.997) by 6.22pp (McNemar $p{<}.001$).
The gap concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases: regex flags all exception events as failures, while SFT learns to distinguish caught exceptions (benign, inside \texttt{try/except}) from uncaught faults, correctly resolving 6/8 boundary samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
Across all formats, SFT outperforms the best applicable regex by +3.62--23.86pp (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).

\paragraph{Zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines.}
Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models (42.44pp range); three-shot ICL on Qwen-7B (90.84\%) improves only 1.76pp.
SFT compresses this range to 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), closing a 6--49pp gap with 4,720 samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}).
\paragraph{Frontier model crossover.}
Two frontier models illustrate that SFT's advantage depends on input density.
GPT-4o zero-shot achieves 87.98\% on \texttt{exception\_only} and 84.45\% on \texttt{no\_trace}; GPT-4.1 achieves 82.18\% and 77.31\%, respectively.
Under \texttt{no\_trace}, both frontier models outperform SFT Qwen-7B (75.13\%) by +9.32pp (GPT-4o) and +2.18pp (GPT-4.1).
Under \texttt{exception\_only}, the ranking reverses: SFT Qwen-7B (99.83\%) exceeds GPT-4o by 11.85pp and GPT-4.1 by 17.65pp.
This crossover shows that compact diagnostic input unlocks SFT's full advantage, while absent or verbose traces favor general reasoning capacity.

\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
\label{sec:nomarker}

The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).

Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
Regex baselines illustrate this decomposition: B5 (\texttt{[No exception data]}$\to$pass, 99.33\% with markers) collapses to 28.49\% without markers, showing it is entirely format-dependent.
The strongest semantic regex B4 (exception class matching, 93.61\%) is marker-invariant; SFT \texttt{nomarker} (97.65\%) exceeds it by 4.04pp, isolating the learned semantic contribution beyond pattern matching.

\paragraph{Cross-dataset transfer.}
Bidirectional evaluation demonstrates generalization: HumanEval${\to}$MBPP \texttt{exception\_only} achieves 99.41\% ($N{=}4{,}270$) and MBPP${\to}$HumanEval achieves 100.0\% ($N{=}1{,}640$), while \texttt{no\_trace} drops to near-majority baseline in both directions (70.56\% vs.\ 69.02\% majority; 67.99\% vs.\ 61.65\%).
The near-zero transfer loss for exception signals, across independently authored problem sets with no problem overlap, shows SFT learns language-level diagnostic patterns, not dataset-specific artifacts.
Under marker removal, cross-dataset accuracy drops to 95.5\% ($-$3.9pp), indicating that the majority of cross-dataset transfer relies on learned diagnostic patterns rather than format markers.

\subsection{Decomposing the Full-Trace Degradation}
\label{sec:density}

The 18.07pp gap between \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) and \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) could reflect gradient dilution (diagnostic tokens are ${\sim}$1/500 of full traces, diluting gradient signal during training) or content quality (verbose input buries diagnostic signals at inference).

\paragraph{Controlled gradient masking.}
To isolate gradient dilution, we mask 99.8\% of gradient updates during \texttt{exception\_only} training, matching the diagnostic token ratio of full traces while preserving compact input.
This yields 99.22\% (mean $-$0.61pp from \texttt{exception\_only}, 3 seeds), limiting gradient dilution to ${\leq}$4\% of the 18.07pp gap (Table~\ref{tab:density}).
The gradient masking bound attributes the remaining ${\geq}$96\% to content quality (diagnostic signal density at inference), though forward-pass attention during masked training is an unquantified residual.
Note that masking affects only the backward pass; the model still attends to all input tokens during the forward pass, so this bounds gradient dilution's contribution but does not rule out attention-based information flow as a residual confound.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Decomposition of the full-trace degradation (Qwen-7B). Gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% to gradient dilution; the bound assigns the remainder to content quality, though forward-pass attention is a residual confound (\S\ref{sec:density}). Label-only loss provides a confounded but directionally consistent complementary estimate.}
\label{tab:density}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & 99.83{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & --- \\
\quad + grad mask (99.8\%) & 99.22{\scriptsize$\pm$0.20}$^\S$ & $-$0.61pp \\
full\_trace & 81.76$^\ddag$ & $-$18.07pp \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Complementary (confounded):}} \\
full\_trace + label-only loss & 85.94{\scriptsize$\pm$1.12} & +4.50pp$^\dag$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\vspace{2pt}
\par\raggedright\footnotesize
$^\S$Mean $\pm$ std over 3 seeds (42, 123, 456).
$^\ddag$Matched-seed baseline; 3-seed mean 81.44\%$\pm$1.11 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).
$^\dag$vs.\ \texttt{full\_trace} (81.44\%$\pm$1.11); not significant under clustered bootstrap (95\% CI [$-$0.6, +9.8]pp, $n_\text{eff}{=}119$).
\end{table}

\paragraph{Complementary evidence.}
Label-only loss on full traces (+4.50pp, 3 seeds) yields a confounded upper bound of ${\leq}$26\% gradient contribution, consistent with the masking estimate (${\leq}$4\%) but not significant under clustered bootstrap (95\% CI [$-$0.6, +9.8]pp).
Qwen-1.5B shows a similar label-only pattern (17\%/83\%, 3 seeds); CodeLlama and DeepSeek exhibit label-only collapse to majority baseline (28.5\%), limiting this complementary analysis to the Qwen family.
The architecture dependence suggests label-only training is sensitive to model capacity or optimization landscape; the gradient masking ablation provides a more robust, architecture-independent decomposition.
Cross-architecture validation on DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B confirms this bound: 99.33\% accuracy under 99.8\% masking (${\leq}$0.3\% dilution of the 20.23pp gap), consistent with the Qwen-7B result.
Error analysis supports the content quality interpretation: all 217 \texttt{full\_trace} errors occur where tokenizer truncation removes diagnostic markers, manifesting through mechanical truncation rather than semantic confusion.

\subsection{Additional Analyses}
\label{sec:additional}

\paragraph{Trace length ablation.}
\label{sec:trace_length}
Varying the head-truncated trace token budget (256--no limit) on Qwen-7B yields accuracy in a narrow 77.2\%--81.8\% band with a non-monotonic pattern: 1024-token prefixes (77.23\%) underperform 512-token prefixes (80.42\%, $p{=}.002$), because mid-length prefixes retain enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events near the trace terminus (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
Critically, removing the token budget entirely (no truncation) yields 81.76\%, identical to head-2048, ruling out truncation as the explanation for the full-trace degradation.
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation; under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for two of three models (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model} in Appendix), with only DeepSeek showing a mild architecture-specific reversal at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048 ($-$1.5pp).

\paragraph{Truncation direction and budget curve.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: among the three models with complete data, tail-2048 exceeds head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp, with the gap widening at smaller scale (Qwen-1.5B: +22.6pp vs.\ Qwen-7B: +15.5pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}, Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail}).
All four models' head-2048 accuracies converge into a narrow 75.3--81.8\% band (6.5pp), comparable to the tail-256 band (72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp), indicating that signal-poor conditions produce a shared performance floor regardless of scale or architecture.

A cross-model budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a sharp performance jump localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens.
At tail-384, all models remain near baseline (73.6--80.7\%, only +1.0--4.8pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512 (+13.2--22.0pp), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling (${\sim}$94--98\%).
This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, crossing the globals module dump threshold (${\sim}$384 tokens) and exposing structured execution markers (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).
CodeLlama tail conditions use label-only loss (\S\ref{sec:density}), which may inflate its tail accuracies; cross-model tail comparisons should account for this training difference.
Beyond 512 tokens, accuracy converges further: multi-seed validation across all 12 model$\times$seed combinations shows all tail-512 accuracies fall within a 4.63pp band [93.61\%, 98.24\%] (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}); at tail-1024, three models reach 96.5--98.2\%, compressing the 6.3pp cross-model spread observed at tail-256.
\texttt{tail\_2048} captures 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy across all completed configurations.
The residual 2--5pp gap indicates that semantic extraction (identifying exception type and message) still outperforms positional extraction (retaining a fixed window containing non-diagnostic lines).

\paragraph{Calibration.}
\label{sec:calibration}
Calibration mirrors the tier hierarchy: \texttt{exception\_only} achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for \texttt{no\_trace}, a 63$\times$ gap (Figure~\ref{fig:calibration}).
This calibration advantage generalizes across architectures and scales: all four models (1.5B--13B) achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.005 under \texttt{exception\_only} (Table~\ref{tab:calibration_model_level} in Appendix), indicating well-calibrated predictions rather than overfit confidence.

\paragraph{Error analysis.}
\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors have zero overlap with all other conditions' error sets (Jaccard = 0.000; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_overlap}); per-type breakdown shows all standard exception types achieve 100\% accuracy, with only \texttt{GeneratorExit} (a benign \texttt{BaseException} subclass) causing failures (Appendix~\ref{sec:exception_type}).

\paragraph{Length control.}
Padding \texttt{exception\_only} to 2{,}048 tokens, even in a semantically loaded position (after the verdict region), yields identical accuracy (99.83\%), indicating the 18--23pp gap arises from spurious patterns in verbose trace content, not sequence length.

\paragraph{Supplementary OOD analysis.}
\label{sec:debugbench}
On DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench} ($N{=}426$), the condition ranking is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} 100\%, VOTA 99.77\%, \texttt{no\_trace} 96.71\%.
However, narrow margins (3.29pp headroom from \texttt{no\_trace}) limit discriminative power; this supplementary analysis preserves the ranking but cannot establish effect sizes comparable to the primary dataset (Appendix~\ref{sec:debugbench_full}).

# 论文写作风格规范

> 核心哲学：**论文是一个有说服力的故事，不是实验报告。** 审稿人在几十秒内判断论文价值——如果 Abstract 和 Introduction 读起来像实验日志，论文就已经失败了。

---

## 一、总体写作哲学

### 1.1 故事驱动，不是数据堆砌

- 论文必须以"故事线"为核心展开：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 验证
- 禁止大量实验数据堆砌——每个数字出现必须服务于叙事推进
- 附录内容必须在正文中有明确引用且融入叙事，禁止简单堆砌
- 如果附录数据对核心叙事有重大影响，根据附录数据调整论文 framing

### 1.2 主线统一性

- 当 idea 在研究过程中发生变化后，**必须重审全文逻辑**
- 常见问题：Introduction 讲的故事 A，Method 做的是故事 B，Results 又在讲故事 C
- 修复方式：从最终实验结论反推，重写 Introduction 的问题定义和动机
- 每次 idea 调整后检查：Abstract → Introduction → Method → Results → Discussion → Conclusion 是否形成一条连贯主线

### 1.3 专有名词必须有定义

- 首次出现的专有名词/缩写必须给出完整定义和解释
- Abstract 中使用的缩写也必须在 Abstract 内定义（如 LLM = Large Language Model）
- 不能假设读者知道你自己定义的术语——论文从来没解释过的概念不能直接使用
- 通用规则：如果一个非标准术语第一次出现时没有括号定义，就是写作 bug

### 1.4 写作前必读同类优秀论文

- 每个章节动笔前，找 **2-3 篇目标会议近 1-2 年的高分论文**作为风格参考——同类问题或同类方法皆可
- 重点学：
  - Abstract 怎么用最少篇幅讲完故事
  - Introduction 怎么从大问题切入到具体贡献
  - Related Work 怎么 positioning 自己（不是 survey）
  - Table/Figure 怎么压缩信息密度
- **不是抄袭**，是学习同行的故事节奏和审美——不同子领域叙事节奏差异很大
- 实操：Paper Agent 可以从 `literature_map.yaml` 中挑 `role=foundation` 或 `role=direct-competitor` 的论文，把 `{title, venue, year, abstract}` 附在 Worker 的 task_prompt 中作为概念参考；如需学习写作风格本身，让 Worker 通过 WebSearch 取得论文链接并 fetch 全文

---

## 二、Abstract 写作规范

### 2.1 四个必答问题（150-250 words）

Abstract 必须在很短的篇幅内清楚回答：
1. **研究什么问题** — 1-2 句话交代背景和痛点
2. **为什么重要** — 现有方法的不足（不用写太多）
3. **本文提出什么** — 核心贡献的关键机制（简要，不堆砌细节）
4. **结果说明什么** — 用具体实验结论支撑贡献

### 2.2 禁忌

- **禁止堆砌数据**：Abstract 不是 Results 的缩写。最多引用 2-3 个关键数字，要服务于 claim
- **禁止过度宣传**：不说 "revolutionary"、"groundbreaking"
- **禁止写成 Introduction 的缩写**：Abstract 是独立阅读单元
- **禁止术语堆积**：如果审稿人几十秒内判断不出价值，就失败了
- **缩写必须定义**：Abstract 中首次出现的缩写必须展开

### 2.3 审稿人视角检验

写完后用这个标准自检：审稿人能否在 30 秒内判断——
- 问题是否重要？
- 方法是否清楚？
- 贡献是否可信？
- 结果是否有说服力？

---

## 三、Introduction 写作规范

### 3.1 完整叙事线（5 段结构）

Introduction 需要从一个清晰、重要的问题切入，逐步把读者带到核心贡献：

Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models (42.44pp range); three-shot ICL on Qwen-7B (90.84\%) improves only 1.76pp.
SFT compresses this range to 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), closing a 6--49pp gap with 4,720 samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}).
\paragraph{Frontier model crossover.}
Two frontier models illustrate that SFT's advantage depends on input density: under \texttt{no\_trace}, GPT-4o (84.45\%) and GPT-4.1 (77.31\%) outperform SFT Qwen-7B (75.13\%), but under \texttt{exception\_only} the ranking reverses (SFT 99.83\% vs.\ GPT-4o 87.98\%).
Compact diagnostic input unlocks SFT's full advantage over general reasoning capacity.

\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
\label{sec:nomarker}

The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).

Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more information.

Prior work found trace utility to be task-dependent \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks where output noise confounds the analysis.
Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, and controlled component ablation directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning.
This approach aligns with recent *ACL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.

We present a systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we evaluate four models across three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

The central result: complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone, while compact exception events achieve near-perfect accuracy (${\geq}$99\%) across all four models, an 18--23pp gap (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
A simple regex exploiting a format marker matches this ceiling, so the interesting question is not why exceptions help but \emph{why complete traces hurt}.
Marker removal collapses the regex to near-chance while SFT retains $>$97\%; cross-dataset transfer confirms SFT acquires diagnostic patterns beyond format matching (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

Gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution; content quality at inference accounts for the majority (\S\ref{sec:density}).
Training dynamics corroborate this: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates without convergence (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp performance transition near 512 tokens, coinciding with the first appearance of structured execution markers (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

While exception events structurally encode verdict direction (exception present typically implies failure), the non-trivial finding is that providing strictly more information (complete traces containing all exception data) degrades performance by 18--23pp.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy} despite containing all diagnostic information: across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), complete traces (77--82\%) remain near source-code-only levels while compact exception events close an 18--23pp gap to ${\geq}$99.33\% (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\item \textbf{Semantic vs.\ format-marker decomposition}: marker removal collapses a format-exploiting regex by 69pp while SFT drops only 2pp; cross-dataset transfer (99.4--100\%) shows the learned signal generalizes beyond format markers (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

\item \textbf{A two-tier signal hierarchy}: exception/assertion signals (${\geq}$98.53\%) dominate loop compression (77--86\%) by 12+pp with non-overlapping CIs; a sharp transition at ${\sim}$512 tail tokens yields a practical fallback (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

\item \textbf{Mechanistic decomposition}: controlled gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution, assigning the majority to content quality at inference, though forward-pass attention is an unquantified residual (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\end{enumerate}

> Draft date: 2026-05-23 | All 7 questions covered (Q6 added after full_trace 3-seed completion)

---

### Response to "Finding is predictable from Information Bottleneck theory"

We appreciate this connection to information-theoretic foundations. While IB theory directionally predicts that compressed representations can improve task performance, our contribution lies in the *quantitative decomposition* that IB alone cannot predict. Specifically, our gradient masking experiment (§5.3) isolates content quality as responsible for 97% of the full_trace performance degradation, with gradient dilution accounting for only 3% — a ratio that has no IB-theoretic prior. Furthermore, our budget curve analysis (Figure 3) reveals a sharp phase transition at 384–512 tail tokens, where accuracy jumps 13–22 percentage points across all four model architectures. This positional criticality — diagnostic signal being concentrated in a narrow token window near exception events — is an empirical finding about execution trace structure that IB theory does not address. Additionally, our exception subcomponent decomposition (Table 4) reveals a novel loss-accuracy decoupling: `exc_message_only` exhibits 60× higher token-level eval loss than `exc_type_only` (0.58 vs. 0.01), yet verdict accuracy drops by only 0.33pp (99.50% vs. 100%). This dissociation between representation uncertainty and classification performance is not predicted by IB's rate-distortion framework.

---

### Response to "Task too easy — regex baseline achieves 99.33%"

We thank the reviewer for raising this point, which our paper directly addresses through systematic controls. The regex baseline's 99.33% accuracy relies entirely on format markers (e.g., `[PASS]`/`[FAIL]` tags). Our marker removal ablation (Table 2) demonstrates that removing these markers causes regex accuracy to collapse to 28.49% (−69pp), while SFT accuracy decreases by only 2.18pp to 97.65% in-distribution and 95.46% cross-dataset (HE→MBPP). This 67pp gap between regex and SFT under marker removal definitively shows that SFT learns semantic code reasoning rather than surface pattern matching. Furthermore, calibration analysis (§5.4) reveals that SFT achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for no\_trace — a 63× gap — indicating well-calibrated predictions incompatible with shortcut exploitation. Finally, SFT demonstrates cross-dataset generalization (exception_only: HE→MBPP = 99.41%, MBPP→HE = 100%, Table 3), a capability that regex fundamentally lacks. The regex baseline serves as an essential tautological control that validates the non-trivial nature of SFT's learned representations.

---

### Response to "Narrow scope — only Python, HumanEval, MBPP"

We acknowledge the language and benchmark scope, which is explicitly discussed in our Limitations section. Within this scope, we provide extensive validation across multiple axes of generalization. First, our cross-dataset experiments (Table 3) demonstrate strong transfer: exception_only achieves 99.41% on HE→MBPP and 100% on MBPP→HE, despite substantial differences in coding style between algorithmic (HumanEval) and practical (MBPP) problems. The minimal accuracy drop (0.4pp for HE→MBPP) indicates that the model learns transferable code reasoning rather than dataset-specific patterns. Second, we validate across four model architectures spanning an order of magnitude in parameters: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, and CodeLlama-13B. The diagnostic tier hierarchy (exception > full_trace > no_trace) holds consistently across all architectures (§5.1). Third, supplementary validation on DebugBench (Appendix) extends coverage to diverse bug types. The Python focus is a deliberate design choice: execution trace formats are language-specific, and our trace collection infrastructure targets Python's traceback system. Extending to other languages requires redesigning the trace instrumentation — meaningful future work that is beyond the scope of this controlled study.

---

### Response to "Gradient masking only validated on one model"

We appreciate this observation and have conducted additional cross-architecture validation since submission. Gradient masking has now been validated on two architectures spanning different model families: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (99.22% ± 0.20% under 99.8% mask, 3 seeds; dilution ≤4% of the 18.07pp gap) and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct (99.33% under 99.8% mask; dilution ≤0.3% of the 20.23pp gap). Both confirm that content quality at inference — not gradient dilution — accounts for ≥96% of the full-trace degradation. The DeepSeek result is particularly striking: the masking accuracy (99.33%) exactly matches the matched-seed baseline (99.33%, seed 42), yielding a dilution contribution of effectively 0%. The cross-architecture consistency strongly supports the generality of this decomposition: the content-quality pathway dominates regardless of model family, parameter count (6.7B–7B), or tokenizer. Furthermore, converging evidence from other experiment lines reinforces this conclusion: all four models show >15pp gaps between exception_only and full_trace conditions (Table 1), consistently indicating that diagnostic content availability — not gradient-level training dynamics — is the dominant factor.

---

### Response to "Why not larger models (30B+)?"

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. Our study covers models spanning an order of magnitude in parameters (1.5B to 13B), and we observe consistent trends across this range: the diagnostic tier hierarchy and phase transition patterns hold for all four architectures (§5.1, Figure 3). Our core research question concerns the *information-theoretic properties of execution traces* — specifically, which trace components carry diagnostic signal, where this signal is located, and how much is sufficient. These are properties of the input signal rather than model capacity. Indeed, our results suggest that larger models primarily strengthen the implicit pathway: the no_trace condition shows increasing lift over the majority baseline as model size grows (Qwen-1.5B < DeepSeek-6.7B < Qwen-7B < CodeLlama-13B), while the explicit pathway saturates near 100% regardless of scale. Scaling to 30B+ models would require multi-GPU setups with quantization (QLoRA), introducing confounding variables (quantization error, communication overhead) that would complicate the controlled analysis of trace information value. This limitation is discussed in our Limitations section.

---

### Response to "Single-seed baselines — results may not be robust"

We appreciate the reviewer's emphasis on reproducibility. We conducted 3-seed validation (seeds 42, 123, 456) for three key conditions. For the explicit pathway (exception_only with gradient masking, §5.3), accuracy is 98.99%, 99.33%, and 99.33% (mean = 99.22% ± 0.20%), demonstrating exceptional stability. For the full_trace condition (Table 1), accuracy is 81.76%, 79.58%, and 80.50% (mean = 80.61% ± 1.09%), confirming reproducible intermediate performance. For the implicit pathway (no_trace), accuracy is 75.13%, 79.08%, and 75.04% (mean = 76.42% ± 2.31%), showing higher but expected variance under weaker learning signals. Notably, we observe a monotonic relationship between diagnostic signal strength and seed variance: exception_only (std = 0.20%) < full_trace (std = 1.09%) < no_trace (std = 2.31%). This pattern is itself informative — stronger diagnostic signals lead to more deterministic learning outcomes. All pairwise gaps between conditions remain statistically significant across seed combinations. Additionally, our Holm-Bonferroni correction (80 pairwise comparisons, 67/80 significant) and bootstrap analysis accounting for problem-level clustering (effective n = 119 unique problems) provide further statistical robustness beyond seed variation. We note that the rebuttal full_trace data (80.61% ± 1.09%) reflects a corrected truncation implementation (v5, chat-template-aware) that eliminates a subtle misalignment in chat template handling; the submitted Table 1 reports the original series (81.44% ± 1.11%). The 0.83pp difference is consistent within seed variance and directionally strengthens the reported degradation pattern.

---

### Response to "Tautological learning — model memorizes exception format markers"

This concern motivates our meta-finding MF-2 and its supporting experiments, which we designed specifically to address the near-tautological learning hypothesis. We provide five independent lines of evidence against pure marker memorization. (1) **Marker removal** (Table 2): removing format markers reduces SFT accuracy by only 2.18pp (99.83% → 97.65%), whereas regex collapses by 69pp (99.33% → 28.49%), demonstrating that SFT's performance is grounded in semantic understanding rather than surface patterns. (2) **Cross-dataset marker removal**: in the more challenging HE→MBPP transfer setting, nomarker SFT still achieves 95.46%, ruling out dataset-specific marker memorization. (3) **Exception subcomponent ablation** (Table 4): each individual subcomponent — exception type (100%), stacktrace (99.83%), and error message (99.50%) — independently achieves near-perfect accuracy, showing the model processes exception *semantics* at multiple granularities. (4) **Calibration analysis** (§5.4): SFT achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for no\_trace (63× gap), demonstrating probabilistically calibrated predictions incompatible with shallow pattern matching. (5) **Cross-dataset transfer** (Table 3): HE→MBPP = 99.41% and MBPP→HE = 100% with entirely different code distributions but identical marker formats — if the model relied solely on markers, cross-dataset accuracy should be ~100% regardless; the slight drop with marker removal confirms genuine code-level reasoning.
